name: Navigate using a compass
blurb: The compass on its own: taking a bearing, walking it accurately, and coming back. Simple in principle, and full of small errors that compound over distance.
gear: An open area to practise in
steps: Learn the parts: the housing, the bezel, the orienting arrow, the direction-of-travel arrow and the magnetic needle.
Learn to take a bearing off an object: point the direction-of-travel arrow at it and rotate the bezel until the needle sits in the shed.
Learn to walk a bearing: pick a distant object on the line, walk to it, and re-shoot. Do not walk while watching the needle.
Learn the back bearing to return along the same line.
Practise a triangle course: three legs of 100 paces at 120-degree bearings should return you to your start. The gap is your error.
Learn to account for magnetic declination in your area, and for the deflection caused by metal near the compass.
tips: Phones, cars, belt buckles and steel-framed glasses all pull the needle. Step away before reading.
Small angular errors become big distance errors. One degree off is about 17 metres per kilometre.
proof: A triangle course of 300 paces returns you within a few metres of your starting point.
